claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially has a high-temperature disordered BCC state.
Elemental segregation during cooling induces local short-range ordering.
Segregation-induced short-range ordering drives decomposition of the high-temperature BCC phase into ordered intermetallic phases such as B2.
Cooling rate controls the extent of selective solute diffusion and segregation.
Al and Cr are particularly involved in selective diffusion and segregation.
Local compositional fluctuations occur preferentially at defect sites or grain boundaries.
Segregated regions mediate nucleation of ordered B2 or other intermetallic regions within the BCC matrix.
Differences in atomic mobility during cooling cause preferential diffusion of Al and Cr.
The resulting compositional inhomogeneities lower local free energy through short-range ordering.
Short-range-ordered regions act as nucleation sites for stable or metastable ordered phases.
Subsequent thermal exposure permits segregated ordered regions to grow and coarsen into distinct intermetallic phases.
Rapid quenching retains the high-temperature disordered BCC structure with minimal segregation and ordering.
Relative to rapid quenching, slow cooling followed by intermediate-temperature holds produces a higher volume fraction of ordered secondary phases such as B2.
Relative to rapid quenching, slow cooling and thermal holds produce more pronounced elemental segregation and ordering.
The proposed pathway requires a regime in which diffusion is active but complete equilibrium has not been reached.
The proposed pathway may be suppressed when quenching is too rapid or temperature is too low for appreciable diffusion.
The proposed pathway may not apply when the composition or cooling conditions drive immediate equilibrium phase separation.
